headline: High risk of cascading errors and capability conflict: transformers can execute/write locally while emqx exposes broad network egress and HTTP APIs, creating unsafe handoff and data-flow pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared channel is documented, so direct prompt injection is not established. However, transformers can read files and run browsers, and emqx exposes HTTP APIs and broad network egress, so a manual or file-based bridge could carry attacker-controlled content. The pathway is plausible but not default.
conditions: IF the operator copies emqx-generated content into transformers prompts or files
IF transformers ingests content from a shared HTTP endpoint without provenance checks
mitigations: Use a separate staging file for any emqx output before feeding transformers
Add a one-line provenance header to all transferred content
Disable browser-based ingestion for untrusted pages
Review copied text for instruction-like payloads before reuse

B_data_leakage.rationale: emqx touches IoT data and has broad network egress, while transformers reads and writes the filesystem and can also egress broadly. A shared workspace or file handoff could move sensitive IoT data into a component that may transmit it onward. The pairwise leakage path exists in common setups, though not proven by direct evidence.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace or exported files
IF IoT data from emqx is written to disk and then loaded by transformers
mitigations: Store emqx exports in a restricted directory
Redact IoT identifiers before handoff
Block outbound network for transformers during local processing
Use separate OS users for each agent
Delete transient files after transfer

C_capability_conflict.rationale: transformers has unrestricted filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and network capabilities, while emqx has broad network egress and HTTP API access. If both operate on the same directory or mutable resources, concurrent writes and side effects can collide. Because no locking or isolation is documented, uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same filesystem path
IF emqx API outputs are consumed while transformers modifies the same artifacts
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Run each agent under a distinct OS account
Disable concurrent writes to shared artifacts
Add file locks around any shared outputs
Use read-only mounts for emqx inputs

D_cascading_error.rationale: transformers can act on files and subprocesses, so it may treat emqx output as authoritative if the orchestrator pipes results directly between them. emqx can emit networked API data, but there is no documented verification step between the agents. The cascade is plausible in default pipelines, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF emqx output is piped into transformers without validation
IF transformers uses emqx-produced text as facts or commands
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents
Require schema checks on all exchanged outputs
Mark emqx output as untrusted by default
Log and diff intermediate artifacts before actioning them

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not request secrets or special OAuth scopes, so no specific residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented. The only compliance-relevant data class named is emqx's IoT data, but there is no evidence that transformers handles a regulated subset or that either agent has a conflicting retention policy. This is a limited, documentation-only gap.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is routed through a non-approved deployment of transformers
IF the operator imposes retention or residency rules not reflected in either profile
mitigations: Confirm data-class handling before deployment
Avoid sending regulated records through the pair
Document retention settings for shared artifacts
Use a local-only environment for sensitive IoT data
